question: How can a survivor of childhood sexual abuse make sense of why Allah let it happen?
answer:
Now, you also in your email ask a very difficult question, which is actually my area. Now you're coming to my area. And that is, you're asking about, as a Muslim, you're struggling with the religious, the theological dimensions of this tragedy, and you're trying to come to terms with some very, very difficult questions. And I wish, dear sister, that I could give you a 30-second response that is watertight, that will eliminate all of those doubts. I wish that I could help you understand those difficult questions of why and how and whatnot, theologically.

But I will tell you that, like you are struggling, not only us as mankind, even the angels struggled in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Even the angels were asking that very difficult question: "Why, O Allah?" Because when Allah announced to the angels that He's creating this new creation called mankind, the angels said, "Why would You create a species, O Allah, that's going to cause so much evil? Why would You do that? They're going to be killing and doing all of these crimes."

> أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا

And what happened to you, sister? That's the fasad that's mentioned. What's happened to you, that's a manifestation of fasad. And fasad is to go beyond the bounds, to hurt people that don't deserve to be hurt. That's the worst type of fasad. And the angels are asking, "O Allah, why would You do that? I want to know." And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala said, basically, essentially: you will have to trust Me. "I know what you don't know."

In other words, even the angels, despite the fact that they have more faith than us and they're more intelligent than us, would not be able to fully understand, philosophically, to get a simple response: why did this happen? Allah said to the angels, "You're going to have to trust Me." And so we begin to answer this question of why with how Allah answered the angels: **you have to begin with a sense of trust.** You have to begin with: you know what? Even if I don't fully understand, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala does. And He created me, and He loves me, and He shall protect me. And what happened was indeed difficult, but even through that, and what I'm seeing now, there's so much positive in my life as well. And I need to concentrate on the positives and work to improve my life, and Allah 'azza wa jall will reward me for the negatives.

So here's the point here: the question of trying to understand why. Some people begin with a very arrogant premise, and they begin with the premise that if I don't understand why, well, then I'm going to blame God, or I'm going to reject God. Literally, that's their paradigm: that if my mind does not comprehend why this happened... Inshallah you are not like this, sister, I know, but I'm saying there are people like this in mankind: if they don't understand why this evil happened, they end up blaming God.

And you know who's the first person to do that? None other than Shaytan himself. Shaytan blamed Allah 'azza wa jall for getting kicked out of heaven. Shaytan blamed Allah for getting misguided, even though, of course, Shaytan was the one in that case. Of course, I mean, this does not apply to that; it's no child's fault. But Shaytan was the one that did what he did, but still he ended up blaming Allah. My point is that we do not blame Allah 'azza wa jall for evils. We don't ascribe evil to Allah. Even if evil exists, we do not ascribe it to Allah, out of respect and adab for Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And we also need to be careful: the assumption that our minds are going to comprehend the wisdom of pain and suffering, the wisdom of evil, that is an assumption that expects our minds to have far more knowledge. Our finite minds can never understand the infinite wisdom of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. However, there are certain things that we can bring.

I want to, by the way, mention an anecdote that happened to me; I met somebody of this nature more than a decade ago. More than a decade ago, I went on an official state delegation from the American State Department, the U.S. State Department, to Auschwitz and Dachau. A group of Muslim clerics and imams, seven, eight of us were chosen, and I was one of them chosen to go to visit Auschwitz and Dachau. This was more than a decade ago: the concentration camps of the Nazis. And because we were an official state delegation, connections were there and whatnot. And so I was very fortunate (and I do say this, fortunate), I was very fortunate to meet some of the Holocaust survivors. All of them have passed away now; this was 10 years ago.

And I met one of them who was in Auschwitz, and he saw the camps. He lived through the camps, and he saw the gas chambers, and he saw his own friends being picked, and he was not picked. There's actually pictures and a video of this somewhere online, I think, because it was all videotaped. He unfolded his arm and showed us the tattoo. Literally, I saw with my own eyes; I was there. There's a picture of that somewhere. The New York Times has an interview with me, and they have that picture there, that I'm looking at this person and he's showing us the tattoo. And then he gave us his story. Mesmerizing. And I have to say, that was one of the most moving times of my life from a non-spiritual perspective. When I say spiritual, I mean like the Haram, Makkah, Madinah, Hajj; that's obviously one genre. Outside of the Haramayn, and outside of that, meeting these types of two, three people we met and hearing their stories, it was just surreal for me.

After that was Q&A. Remember, this is a man that has lived through Auschwitz and Dachau. I was the first to raise my hand, and I said, "You are from a Jewish background. How did your experiences affect your faith? How did your experiences affect your faith?" And his answer was disappointing. And I'm going to say it, because we need to learn from the good and the bad of all the people. We need to learn from their good and their bad. And this was a mistake that he made, and it was something that we have to learn from.

His face scowled. I mean, in one sense, he's literally gone through the Nazi extermination camps. He's literally seen what, what percentage would have seen this, right? His face scowled, and he said, a'udhu billah, he said, "There is no God." And he said, "My experiences in Auschwitz made me give up my faith. What I saw made me give up my faith."

And that is one possibility of somebody that goes through trauma. But Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says in the Qur'an that there are two types of people. There's one type that, if bad happens, basically turns away from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. They worship Allah conditionally: if bad happens to him, he turns his back and walks away, and if good happens, then and only then he worships Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. You see, we worship Allah through thick and thin. We worship Allah through times of difficulty and times of ease. We worship Allah regardless, because He is worthy of being worshipped.

And even if I cannot understand something that has happened to me, it does not negate all of the other blessings. It does not negate my life, the air that I breathe, the family and friends that I have, the life that I live. And most importantly, it does not negate the existence of God Himself, or the existence of the rewards and pleasures of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

So I wish I could have a simple answer to answer your difficult question. All I can say is that there must be a sense of trust. Allah 'azza wa jall says in the Qur'an: no soul is burdened with something more than what it can bear. And so you might have been burdened with more than what many other souls can bear, but you were not burdened with more than what you could bear. And here you are now, strong, powerful, having gone through all of what you've gone through, and you're still alive. You've made it through that difficult, dark tunnel, and here you are, and you have the rest of your life ahead of you. And Allah 'azza wa jall knows what that life holds.

So look back, but don't dwell. Look back, but then turn away and walk forward, benefiting from your wisdom and maturity, your courage and bravery. Let your experiences shape you, but don't define you. Let your experiences shape you for the better, but don't be defined by your past. And know that for every negative that happens to you, there's always two positives. Know that for every difficulty, there's going to be multiple blessings in your life, and the more the difficulties, the more the blessings.

Dear sister in Islam, I have no doubt... I don't know you, I don't know your name; the email was anonymous as well. I don't know anything about you, but I know one thing: Allah's promise is true. And that promise tells me that because of all the negatives that you've had in your life, you must have so many positives as well, and those positives will far outweigh the negatives. But unfortunately, our problem, my problem, is that when a small ant bites me, I neglect the beauty around me. And I'm not trying to trivialize your problem; I'm saying to myself, if something small happens, I trivialize the beauty around me. So in your case, it wasn't something small. It was very, very traumatic. It was very big. But Allah 'azza wa jall put you through it knowing that there is something on the other side that will be better for you, in this world and then the next as well.

Because here's the point: I can understand, honestly, I can understand if somebody doesn't believe in a hereafter, and Auschwitz happens, the Nazi concentration camps happen, or this happens; in their world, they don't understand why, they reject God. But see, here's the point: as Muslims, we don't believe that this life is the end. We believe that there is a next life. So how can anybody who believes in a next life end up rejecting Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala? Because it's the next life where the good shall be rewarded for their good, and the evil shall be punished for their evil.

Dear sister, one of the ways you need to overcome what happened in the past is to think of the future. And by future I don't mean tomorrow; I mean the Day of Judgment future. I mean when you will stand in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and you will be rewarded infinitely more than you can imagine for your patience. And when you will stand in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and you will be able to point at your perpetrator in front of the court of Allah on the Day of Judgment, when Allah shall be on His throne judging the creation, and you will be able to point at your perpetrator and say, "That man did such and such." Now it's his turn to be punished, and the satisfaction you will get.

Because here's the point, dear sister: wallahi, whatever happens to that man in this world, thrown in jail or this or that, it's not enough. That's not justice. So what if he goes to jail and has three meals a day and air to breathe and TV to watch? How is that a commensurate punishment for the trauma that he has caused a little girl? Think about that. It's only Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala that can deal with justice the way that justice should be dealt with. It is Allah 'azza wa jall who serves ultimate justice, and that is why we have to wait for that day to receive that ultimate justice.

There's a beautiful hadith in the Sunan Ibn Majah. When the cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, returned to Madinah (the Prophet ﷺ really liked him; he was his favorite cousin, one of his favorite cousins, a very friendly relationship between him and Ja'far radiAllahu 'anhu), he asked Ja'far radiAllahu 'anhu, "Tell me some of the stories. Tell me some of the strange things you saw in Habasha, in Abyssinia." And so Ja'far gave this story. He said, "O Messenger of Allah, one day there was an elderly lady from the clergy class, from the righteous religious folks amongst them, and she was carrying a jug of water. And a group of hooligans, a group of ruffians, young men from a higher socioeconomic class basically, saw her and began mocking her. And one of them came and pushed her so hard that she fell down on her back, and the jug of water crashed (that difficult water she was carrying, it crashed), and they all began laughing around her."

And she's an elderly lady. What's going to happen? There must have been socioeconomic differences, there must have been ethnic divides, there must also be that notion of making fun of religious folks. All of this is being compounded. So she turns around in her anger and she says, "You traitor," or "you evil person, what will you do on the day that Allah shall bring His kursi out and shall gather all of mankind in front of Him, and every single person's limbs will testify in front of Allah of what they used to do? Where will you find protection? On that day I shall have a case against you. On that day you will see what's going to happen between us."

The Prophet ﷺ confirmed the truth of what that elderly Abyssinian lady said. She had no help in this world. In this world, these ruffians, the hooligans, managed to make fun of her, laugh at her, mock her, and in her anger she could not say anything except wait till the Day of Judgment. And you know what our Prophet ﷺ said? "Sadaqat. She has spoken the truth. She has spoken the truth. How will Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala honor a people that does not take care of their weak against their powerful?" SubhanAllah, he affirmed the words of the old lady.

If an old lady can complain on the Day of Judgment about a group of young men who pushed her and broke her water jug, then what do you think about a little girl who was violated repeatedly by somebody whom she was supposed to trust, and somebody who claimed to love her? What do you think will be the affair of that person?

Dear sister, and through you all brothers and sisters, take consolation that there's something called Judgment Day. You must, because it will keep your sanity. You must, because this is how you're going to contextualize what is happening. You must, because that is your only salvation. That is your ultimate justice. Not necessarily this world; this world might be partial justice. But it is on the Day of Judgment that you will get your full rewards, and your perpetrators will face the wrath of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And especially for a crime of this nature: a compounded crime, a crime of innocence, a crime involving a young child, a crime of penetration, of intercourse, a crime of non-consensual, of a minor, of a life ruined. Wallahi, how can such a person... I mean, we leave the repentance to Allah. I should not say anything more than this. But no doubt, this is a major, major, major sin. No doubt, what this person has done really checks all the boxes of a major sin. And this is something that they will have to stand in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala for, and Allah 'azza wa jall will deal with them the way that they deserve to be dealt with.

So in trying to cope with these thoughts of yours, of why and how, I urge you to find the answer not necessarily logically, but spiritually. Let your heart answer you. Let your heart connect with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and find an answer that is in the joy of iman in Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. That will be more powerful than any pseudo-rational or intellectual response, because at the end of the day, Allah said to the angels, "I know what you do not know."
